summary: Researched via web search and page fetches only. Screen, power and FSR prices are seen on pages. The key finding for the keybed is negative: I could not find any shop listing a 25-key velocity mini-key mechanism as a standalone part with price and key pitch. Small makers appear to go through OEM contact (Fatar/Doepfer for full-size keybeds) or cannibalise a cheap 25-key controller. Pads: no ready 16-pad velocity PCB or silicone set with a price was found; only single FSRs (Adafruit) and DIY/salvaged MPC-pad builds. Daisy Seed has 31 GPIO (D0-D30) per the v1.0.5 datasheet, enough for a 16-bit parallel screen only if little else is used; SPI is the practical choice. Items marked estimate are my arithmetic or reasoning, not read on a page.
price_read: Seen prices: 4in ST7796S SPI display 13.50 USD at 1 (Elecrow), 3.5in IPS ILI9488 8.34 USD at 100 (BuyDisplay), charger+5V boost module 7.16 USD at 100 (Adafruit bq25185 board; module, not IC-level), single FSR 5.95 USD each at 1 (Adafruit; 16 would be about 95 USD, which is why a bought FSR per pad is not viable). Complete 25-key velocity mini controllers retail around 50-100 USD (Nektar SE25 49.99 USD listed out of stock, Roland K-25m 99 USD new at Thomann, Arturia MiniLab 3 94 EUR), so a bare mini keybed at volume is plausibly 10-20 USD (estimate, no page states it). Not priced from any page: STM32H750 MCU, codec, SD slot, USB-C, TRS jack, encoders, cell, enclosure, PCB assembly. With screen about 9-14, charger section about 3-7, keybed about 10-20 (est.), pads about 5-15 via custom conductive-rubber plus FSR film (est.), the four sourced categories alone are about 27-56 USD before MCU, audio, connectors, 3000 mAh cell, case and assembly. My honest read is that an 80 USD BOM is too tight for keybed + 16 pads + colour screen + battery; 100-130 USD is more realistic (estimate). At roughly 2.5-3x BOM to retail, that points to about 250-330 USD, so the 250 USD ceiling is only reachable with a cost-downed design (SPI screen of 3.5in, in-house pad sheet, no fuel gauge) and thin margin. Treat 150-250 as achievable only at the top of the range.

categories.title: Keybed (25 key velocity)
categories.note: No standalone 25-key velocity mini-key mechanism with a posted price and key pitch was found. Doepfer sells bare Fatar keybeds per a 2007 forum post (stale; 88/76 key) with two contacts per note on make/break bus bars. A 2018-era Velokeys page confirms the two-switch-per-key velocity principle. Key pitch/octave width in mm was not stated on any page I read for mini keys (Roland K-25m page gives only overall 308 x 209 x 44 mm; Akai MPK Mini 318 x 181 x 44 mm; Arturia MiniLab 3 355 x 220 x 50 mm). Prices below are retail of complete controllers; the cheapest ones are the best prototype donors.

options.name: Fatar/Doepfer bare keybed (full-size)
options.vendor: Doepfer (via forum post) / Elby Designs page
options.specs: Fatar TP10MDF without electronics, two contacts per note on make and break bus bars; thread dated 2007, 88 and 76 key then; Elby page describes a Fatar 49-key unweighted keybed 684 x 162 mm. No 25-key mini option and no price seen.
options.fit: Right interface (matrix, two contacts) but full-size keys, wrong size and no price, so only useful as the reference scheme.

options.name: Nektar SE25 (25 velocity mini keys)
options.specs: 25 velocity-sensitive mini keys, 3 velocity curves, USB class compliant. Page showed it currently unavailable. Key pitch not stated.
options.fit: Cheapest complete 25-key donor for prototype keybed reuse, but check stock and the actual key pitch with a ruler before buying.

options.name: Roland K-25m keyboard unit
options.specs: 25 velocity-sensitive keys; B-stock 93, new listed at 99. Roland page gives 308 x 209 x 44 mm; key size not stated.
options.fit: Compact body, keyboard-only (no pads), good donor if the key feel tests better than the Nektar.

options.name: Korg nanoKEY2
options.specs: 25 velocity keys, 12.80 x 3.27 x 0.65 in. Price seen 122.95 CAD (not converted). Slim keys are likely too small for this project.
options.fit: Not recommended: keys are the very thing we are trying to improve on.

options.name: Arturia MiniLab 3
options.specs: 25 velocity mini keys, 8 pads, 355 x 50 x 220 mm, 94 EUR incl. VAT (not converted).
options.fit: Useful as a size reference for a larger-than-mini-key target; the pads are also reusable for testing.

options.name: Akai MPK Mini MK3
options.specs: 25 compact velocity keys, 16 pads (8 x 2 banks per page), 318 x 181 x 44 mm. Price not on page.
options.fit: Same key class as the FM-1 problem; use only as a comparison case.

categories.title: 16 velocity pads
categories.note: No ready 16-pad PCB or silicone pad set with a price was found. Seen: single square FSR at Adafruit, and a DIY MPC-style 4x4 build that scans FSRs with a 16-channel mux (HCF4067) into one analog pin, 10k pull-down. Typical scan: FSR in a divider into an ADC, via an analog mux. Piezo options were not priced from any page.

options.name: Square Force-Sensitive Resistor (FSR) Alpha MF02A-N-221-A01
options.specs: 38 mm square sensing area, 87.18 x 43.7 mm, 0.55 mm thick, 1 to 49 N; no quantity pricing listed. 16 would be about 95 USD at 1.
options.fit: Good for a prototype with a few pads, too expensive as 16 discrete sensors; a product would need a printed FSR sheet.

options.name: DIY MPC-style 4x4 FSR controller
options.specs: Salvaged Akai MPC 2000 pads on FSRs, ~1.25 in pads with ~0.125-0.25 in gaps, HCF4067 mux, 10k divider, one ADC pin. Author found 8 USD per commercial FSR too expensive for 16.
options.fit: Proves the scan circuit (mux into the Daisy ADC, which has 12 inputs) and gives a prototype path; no price for a buyable pad set.

options.name: Custom printed FSR sheet + silicone pad mat
options.specs: No vendor or price found. This is the likely production route (my reasoning, not a page).
options.fit: Needs an RFQ to a Chinese membrane switch maker; cannot be priced from public pages.

categories.title: Colour screen (3.2 to 4.3 in)
categories.note: Refresh rate: SPI at 40 MHz moves 480x320x16 bit = 2.46 Mbit per full frame, so roughly 16 fps full-screen at 40 MHz and more if partial updates are used (estimate by arithmetic; Daisy SPI speed limits not read). 8/16-bit 8080 parallel via FMC or GPIO is several times faster but costs 11-19+ pins. Daisy Seed datasheet v1.0.5: 31 GPIO (D0-D30), 12 ADC inputs, 2 DAC, SPI1 on D7-D10, SPI3 and SPI2_NSS available, SAI2 used for audio, no FMC mentioned. Estimate: with 16 pad ADC, 25-key matrix (or mux), encoders, SD (sdmmc), MIDI UART and USB, parallel would be a squeeze; use SPI on Daisy and FMC on the custom board.

options.name: 4.0in 480x320 SPI TFT, ST7796S
options.specs: 480x320, 65K colour, 4-wire SPI, 3.3 V, active area 55.68 x 83.52 mm, module 61.74 x 108.04 mm, optional XPT2046 touch. No volume tiers (contact for OEM).
options.fit: Easiest prototype screen on Daisy SPI; page does not say IPS.

options.name: 4in 320x480 SPI TFT, ST7796S
options.specs: Price seen 18.00 EUR at 1, 17.75 at 10+, 17.00 at 100+ (not converted). Resistive touch; 107 x 62 mm. IPS not stated; page warns the wrong driver may be printed on the PCB.
options.fit: Same class as Elecrow; shows the cost of a resold module is near 17-18 EUR at 100.

options.name: 3.5in IPS 320x480 TFT, ILI9488, bare panel
options.specs: IPS, ILI9488, interfaces: RGB, 3/4-wire SPI, 8080 8/9/16-bit; outline 54.5 x 83.0 mm, active 48.96 x 73.44 mm; 9.10 at 10, 8.85 at 30, 8.61 at 50, 8.34 at 100, 500+ by quote; no single-unit price listed.
options.fit: Best volume price and supports SPI now and 16-bit parallel later on the custom board; 3.5in is small versus the 4in target.

categories.title: Battery and power
categories.note: Runtime arithmetic (estimate): 3000 mAh x 3.7 V = 11.1 Wh. At 1.5 W average and 100% conversion that is 7.4 h. With a boost/buck chain of about 85% efficiency (assumed) usable energy is 9.4 Wh, so about 6.3 h. Cell derating to about 90% of rated capacity at that load gives about 5.7 h. Charging takes about 3 h at 1 A. No fuel gauge module was priced.

options.name: Adafruit bq25185 USB / DC / Solar Charger with 5V Boost
options.specs: USB-C in, 1 A charge default (500 mA by jumper), 5 V boost up to 1 A, TPS61023 boost, power-path, JST PH battery connector; 8.95 at 1-9, 8.06 at 10-99, 7.16 at 100+. Page itself warns of possible stall above 200 mA with resistive loads at power-up. 1 A may be marginal for a 1.5 W (about 300 mA at 5 V) design plus screen backlight and charge.
options.fit: Good prototype power board feeding the Daisy VIN; for the product use the bq25185 and TPS61023 on the main PCB, which will cost much less than the module.

options.name: PSM-206-2A USB-C 18650 charge and boost module
options.specs: Page described 5 V/2 A boost output; price, charge current and IC were not visible in the fetched part of the page.
options.fit: Possible cheap alternative with more output current, but unverified specs, so not a basis for a design.
